```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7.2, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 144, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")
library(idiographic)
data(srl)
analysis_data <- subset(srl, name %in% c("Aisha", "Alice", "Anika", "Astrid", "Bjorn", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana", "Erik", "Eve", "Fatima", "Frank"))
```

An idiographic model is estimated from the observations of a single person,
so the quality of that person's data limits what the model can show. Before
any model is fitted, descriptive statistics are therefore computed separately
for each person and each variable. These are the number of observations and
missing values, the spacing of the occasions, the mean and the range, the
standard deviation, the change from one occasion to the next, and the
correlation of each occasion with the previous one. These statistics establish
whether the data of each person can be analysed and reveal the problems that
would distort the results.

The first problem is a short series. Every coefficient of a person's model is
estimated from that person's observations alone, and a series with few
observations gives unstable estimates and supports only a small model. Missing
occasions and long gaps between occasions shorten the series further and break
the regular spacing that lagged effects assume, because a lag that spans one
day for one pair of observations and a week for another mixes two different
quantities.

The second problem is low variability. A variable that changes little within a
person carries little information about its effects, and its coefficient has a
wide confidence interval. A variable that is constant within a person cannot be
estimated as a predictor at all. Responses gathered at the floor or ceiling of
the scale restrict the range in the same way and weaken the observed
associations.

The third problem is dependence over time. A series with a trend changes level
over the study period, and two variables that both trend appear related even
when their daily fluctuations are unrelated. A series with strong
autocorrelation carries each day's value into the next day, so its
observations are less informative than their number suggests. Long runs of
identical responses can indicate careless responding.

The fourth problem concerns the level of the variation. Part of the variance of
a variable lies between persons, in their means, and part lies within persons,
in their daily fluctuations. A correlation computed across all observations
mixes the two parts, and the share of each determines whether the variable is
suited to a within-person analysis.

## Data

```{r data-values, include = FALSE}
n_learners <- length(unique(analysis_data$name))
n_days <- length(unique(analysis_data$day))
```

The examples use `r n_learners` learners from `srl`, a data frame in long
format with one row per learner and day. Each learner rated self-efficacy,
effort and seven other indicators of self-regulated learning once a day for
`r n_days` days.

## Level and variability

Level and variability are the basic properties of a time series. The level is
the typical value of a person's responses, given by the mean and the median.
The variability is the amount by which the responses change over time, and it
determines how much the series can show about the effects of its variable. A
variable that stays at nearly the same value for `r n_days` days shows little
of what happens when it changes.

The variability of each series is measured in two ways. The standard deviation
(SD) measures the spread of a person's observations around that person's mean
over the whole study. The root mean square successive difference (RMSSD)
measures the size of the change from one occasion to the next. A series that
drifts slowly over a wide range and a series that alternates sharply from day
to day can have the same SD, and the second has the larger RMSSD
[@jahng2008]. The two are linked by the lag-1 autocorrelation $\rho_1$, the
correlation of each occasion with the previous one. For a stationary series
$\text{RMSSD} \approx \text{SD}\sqrt{2(1-\rho_1)}$, so the RMSSD is about 1.41
times the SD when consecutive days are unrelated, and smaller when each day
carries over into the next.

`describe_persons()` returns one row per person and variable, with the number
of observations, the missing values, the span of the occasions and the gaps
between them, the level and the variability. The argument `time` orders the
observations, and the successive differences and the autocorrelation are
computed in that order.

```{r description-table}
describe_persons(analysis_data, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "effort"),
                 time = "day", subject = c("Aisha", "Alice"))
```

```{r description-values, include = FALSE}
two_learners <- as.data.frame(describe_persons(
  analysis_data, id = "name", vars = "efficacy", time = "day",
  subject = c("Aisha", "Alice")
))
aisha <- subset(two_learners, subject == "Aisha")
alice <- subset(two_learners, subject == "Alice")
whole <- \(x) sprintf("%.0f", x)
```

Aisha and Alice each have `r aisha$n` observations and no missing values.
Their mean efficacy is `r whole(aisha$mean)` and `r whole(alice$mean)`, both
have an SD of `r whole(aisha$sd)`, and their RMSSDs are `r whole(aisha$rmssd)`
and `r whole(alice$rmssd)`. The two learners differ in their typical level of
efficacy and have similar day-to-day variability.

The figure plots the SD against the RMSSD for the `r n_learners` learners,
with one point per learner and variable.

```{r description-plot, fig.cap="Figure 1. Spread (SD) against day-to-day change (RMSSD) for efficacy and effort in 12 learners."}
descriptives <- describe_persons(analysis_data, id = "name",
                                 vars = c("efficacy", "effort"), time = "day")
plot_descriptives(descriptives)
```

```{r description-ratio, include = FALSE}
descriptive_table <- as.data.frame(descriptives)
ratio <- sprintf("%.2f", range(descriptive_table$rmssd / descriptive_table$sd))
```

The RMSSD lies between `r ratio[1]` and `r ratio[2]` times the SD, close to the
value of 1.41 for unrelated consecutive days, so the learners carry little over
from one day to the next. Erik and Eve have the largest spread and the largest
daily change in both efficacy and effort. Diana, Frank and Bob vary least in
efficacy, and Frank's effort is among the most variable, so a learner can be
stable on one variable and variable on another.

With `detail = "full"`, the table adds the proportions of responses at the
floor and ceiling of the scale, the skewness and kurtosis, the probability of
an acute change between consecutive occasions, the linear trend over the study
and the longest run of identical responses. These columns detect the
restricted range, the trends and the careless responding described above.
Missing occasions reduce the number of consecutive pairs from which the RMSSD
and the autocorrelation are computed.

## Within-person correlations

```{r correlation-values, include = FALSE}
pooled_r <- cor(analysis_data$monitoring, analysis_data$effort,
                use = "complete.obs")
person_r <- as.data.frame(correlate_persons(
  analysis_data, id = "name", vars = c("monitoring", "effort"), time = "day"
))$r
two_dp <- \(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
signed <- \(x) sub("^-", "−", two_dp(x))
```

A within-person correlation quantifies the covariation of two variables across
the occasions of one person. It indicates which states co-occur within an
individual, and its sign and magnitude differ between individuals. A
correlation computed over the pooled observations of a sample combines
within-person and between-person covariation, and it can differ from the
within-person correlation of every individual in the sample. In the pooled
observations of the `r n_learners` learners, monitoring and effort correlate
at `r two_dp(pooled_r)`. The within-person correlations of the same pair range
from `r signed(min(person_r))` to `r signed(max(person_r))` and are negative
for `r sum(person_r < 0)` of the `r n_learners` learners.

The within-person correlation is the Pearson correlation of two variables
computed from the observations of one person. A positive correlation indicates
that on occasions when one variable exceeds the person's mean, the other
variable also tends to exceed its mean. `correlate_persons()` returns one row
per person and pair of variables, with the correlation, the number of complete
pairs and a 95% confidence interval based on Fisher's $z$ transformation.

```{r correlation-table}
correlations <- correlate_persons(analysis_data, id = "name",
                                  vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"),
                                  time = "day", subject = c("Aisha", "Alice"))
correlations
```

```{r correlation-pairs, include = FALSE}
pair_r <- as.data.frame(correlations)
aisha_r <- subset(pair_r, subject == "Aisha")$r
alice_pair <- \(a, b) subset(pair_r, subject == "Alice" & x == a & y == b)$r
```

For Aisha, all three pairs are positively correlated, with coefficients between
`r two_dp(min(aisha_r))` and `r two_dp(max(aisha_r))`. For Alice, efficacy and
effort are positively correlated (r = `r two_dp(alice_pair("efficacy", "effort"))`),
and monitoring is negatively correlated with efficacy
(r = `r signed(alice_pair("efficacy", "monitoring"))`) and with effort
(r = `r signed(alice_pair("monitoring", "effort"))`). Alice reports lower
effort and lower efficacy on occasions of higher monitoring.

The figure plots each correlation with its 95% confidence interval, ordered by
magnitude.

```{r correlation-plot, fig.cap="Figure 2. Within-person correlations with 95% confidence intervals for two learners."}
plot_correlations(correlations)
```

```{r correlation-intervals, include = FALSE}
one_side <- sum(pair_r$conf_low > 0 | pair_r$conf_high < 0)
```

Of the `r nrow(pair_r)` intervals, `r one_side` lie entirely on one side of
zero.

The coefficients describe concurrent associations, measured on the same
occasion, and each is a bivariate association unadjusted for the remaining
variables. Temporal precedence is examined with lagged regressions and dynamic
networks. Serial dependence between consecutive daily observations makes the
confidence intervals too narrow when the autocorrelation is strong. The
argument `min_n` sets the minimum number of complete pairs for a coefficient to
be reported, and a variable that is constant within a person yields a missing
coefficient.

## Between-person and within-person variance

Person-specific models use only the fluctuation of each person around that
person's mean. Analyses that combine persons, such as pooled regressions,
multilevel models and the comparison of individual with pooled estimates, use
both the differences between person means and the fluctuation within persons.
For these analyses, the partition of the variance determines how each variable
enters the model. Between-person variance arises from differences in the
person means, and within-person variance arises from the fluctuation of each
person around that person's mean.

The intraclass correlation (ICC) is the between-person share of the total
variance. A large ICC indicates that much of the variance reflects stable
differences between persons. An association computed on the raw scores of all
persons is then largely an association between person means. Such a variable
enters a pooled analysis as a person mean and a deviation from it, so that the
within-person and between-person effects are estimated separately with
`split_levels()` and `fit_within_between()`. The ICC is a property of the
sample, computed over all persons. The within-person variability of an
individual is assessed with the SD and RMSSD of that individual's series. The
reliability of the person means indicates how precisely the between-person
part of a variable is measured, and an unreliable person mean biases the
between-person and contextual effects.

```{r variance-table}
components <- variance_components(analysis_data, id = "name",
                                  vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"))
components
```

```{r variance-values, include = FALSE}
component_table <- as.data.frame(components)
icc_of <- \(v) two_dp(subset(component_table, variable == v)$icc)
within_pct <- sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * range(1 - component_table$icc))
min_reliability <- floor(100 * min(component_table$reliability)) / 100
mean_obs <- round(mean(component_table$n / component_table$people))
```

The ICCs are `r icc_of("efficacy")` for efficacy, `r icc_of("monitoring")` for
monitoring and `r icc_of("effort")` for effort, so between `r within_pct[1]`
and `r within_pct[2]` of the variance of each variable lies within learners,
the part that person-specific models use. The between-person share is
substantial for all three variables, and in a pooled analysis each is
decomposed into a person mean and a deviation before entering the model. The
reliability of the person means exceeds `r two_dp(min_reliability)` for all
three variables, because each mean is computed from about `r mean_obs`
observations.

The figure plots the between-person and within-person share of the variance of
each variable.

```{r variance-plot, fig.cap="Figure 3. Between-person and within-person shares of variance."}
plot_variance(components)
```

A variable that is constant within persons supports only between-person
comparisons, and a variable without between-person variance supports only
within-person analysis.

## Within-person and between-person correlations

Findings obtained from a group are often taken to describe the individuals in
that group. The inference from the group to the individual holds when the
process is ergodic, that is, when the relations among the variables are the
same within every person and stable over time [@molenaar2004]. Fisher,
Medaglia and Jeronimus [-@fisher2018] proposed a direct test of this
generalisation for correlations. For one pair of variables, two distributions
of correlations are compared. The within-person distribution contains one
correlation per person, computed across that person's occasions. The
between-person distribution contains one correlation per occasion, computed
across persons. The first observations of all persons form one
cross-sectional sample, the second observations form a second one, and so on.
When group-level results generalise to individuals, the two distributions have
similar means and similar spreads. Across six samples, Fisher and colleagues
found the within-person standard deviation to be two to four times the
between-person standard deviation.

```{r levels-values, include = FALSE}
all_learners <- length(unique(srl$name))
all_days <- length(unique(srl$day))
```

The comparison uses all `r all_learners` learners in `srl`, so each
between-person correlation rests on `r all_learners` persons and each
within-person correlation on up to `r all_days` occasions.
`correlate_levels()` returns one row per pair of variables, with the mean and
standard deviation of each distribution and the ratio of the two standard
deviations.

```{r levels-table}
levels_result <- correlate_levels(srl, id = "name",
                                  vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"),
                                  time = "day")
levels_result
```

```{r levels-summary, include = FALSE}
level_table <- as.data.frame(summary(levels_result))
pair_of <- \(a, b) subset(level_table, x == a & y == b)
eff_mon <- pair_of("efficacy", "monitoring")
mon_eff <- pair_of("monitoring", "effort")
eff_eff <- pair_of("efficacy", "effort")
sd_ratio <- two_dp(range(level_table$sd_ratio))
```

For efficacy and monitoring, and for monitoring and effort, the mean
correlations at the two levels are close (`r two_dp(eff_mon$mean_within)` and
`r two_dp(eff_mon$mean_between)`; `r two_dp(mon_eff$mean_within)` and
`r two_dp(mon_eff$mean_between)`). For efficacy and effort, the mean
within-person correlation (`r two_dp(eff_eff$mean_within)`) is lower than the
mean between-person correlation (`r two_dp(eff_eff$mean_between)`). For all
three pairs, the within-person correlations are more dispersed, with a
standard deviation `r sd_ratio[1]` to `r sd_ratio[2]` times that of the
between-person correlations. For two of the three pairs, the correlation
across learners approximates the average within-learner correlation, and the
correlations of the individual learners are distributed about twice as widely
around it.

The figure plots the two distributions as density curves. The ticks below each
curve mark the individual correlations, and the vertical lines mark the means.

```{r levels-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Figure 4. Distributions of within-person correlations (one per learner, solid) and between-person correlations (one per occasion, dashed) for three pairs of variables."}
plot_levels(levels_result)
```

Serial dependence within persons can inflate the spread of the within-person
correlations. With `lag_adjust = TRUE`, each variable is first regressed on its
own lag-1 value and on the lag-1 value of the other variable, and the
within-person correlations are computed from the residuals.

```{r levels-lag}
lagged_levels <- correlate_levels(srl, id = "name",
                                  vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"),
                                  time = "day", lag_adjust = TRUE)
summary(lagged_levels)
```

```{r levels-lag-values, include = FALSE}
lagged_table <- as.data.frame(summary(lagged_levels))
shift <- merge(level_table, lagged_table, by = c("x", "y"),
               suffixes = c("", "_lag"))
max_shift <- sprintf("%.3f", max(abs(shift$mean_within_lag - shift$mean_within)))
lag_ratio <- two_dp(range(lagged_table$sd_ratio))
```

The adjustment changes the mean within-person correlations by at most
`r max_shift`, and the ratios of the standard deviations remain between
`r lag_ratio[1]` and `r lag_ratio[2]`. The lag-1 autocorrelations in Figure 1
are small, and the larger spread of the within-person correlations reflects
differences between learners in the covariation of the variables.

The between-person correlations require occasions that are comparable across
persons, and here the $t$-th observation of every learner is treated as one
occasion. With few persons, each between-person correlation rests on a small
sample, and its sampling error adds to the between-person spread. The ratio of
the standard deviations is a descriptive index and is reported without a
significance test.

## From description to models

The descriptions identify the persons and variables that can be analysed and
the form in which the variables enter the models. Series that are short,
sparse or nearly constant are excluded or analysed with fewer predictors.
Variables with a substantial between-person share are decomposed into person
means and deviations. The within-person correlations and their spread indicate
how far a pooled estimate describes the individual learners. The
person-specific estimates are then modelled and compared with the pooled
estimate using `fit_lm()`, `fit_within_between()` and `pool_coefs()`.
